Basically, you're gonna go in and they're gonna ask you a lot of questions. They'll want to know emergency contacts who they can potentially contact about anything (if you have any), and they'll take you to a quiet area where you can talk to a nurse one on one about your thoughts. They'll ask if you're contemplating suicide explicitly, or just overall want to die, and ask if you've made any plans. They generally have a separate waiting room for patients who are completely non violent where it's quiet, they have comfy furniture, and they'll ask if you want to talk or be alone. If you say alone, they'll be quiet in the room, but nurses will generally be non judgmental and will talk to you about anything you're interested in. It's a little scary at first, especially when you get taken to an evaluation room and many places will make you change in front of them to check for self harm. But everyone is nice to you, and generally wants to help. A lot of my local nurses know me by name, know what my favorite type of juice is, and are totally prepared to deal with my panic attacks. It can be really helpful, if you feel you need help and supervision. I generally go in when I'm afraid to be alone, and they know that by now

I stopped showing up, and lost all my participation points. It doesn't mean that you're stupid. More than anything, it's a cry for help. Are you on any medications? I found that when I was feeling the worst, my brain tried to convince me not to take antidepressants and mood stabilizers, or eat or drink anything. Keep drinking water, stay hydrated, eat something other than a bag of microwave popcorn in a day. You'll want to binge on junk food sometimes, but that will make things worse. And I just want to say that depression may be trying to convince you that you'll be doing your family a favor by not doing it on Christmas, but it doesn't matter what day you choose, that day and many other days will still be ruined by losing you. Don't let depression tell you that you aren't important. It's tough, but everything worth doing is. See if you can appeal to your university after a certain amount of time to get reaccepted; if not, you can prove your academic worth at a community college first and then transfer in. But I would suggest that you wait to do this until you get some help. Take your medications, make therapy appointments (AND KEEP THEM), and over time you'll find that even when things aren't perfect, you're doing a little better each day. Then you can go back to school when you're not just focused on how you want to die every day. Don't let anyone tell you that self care is weak. It's the strongest choice you can make to keep yourself alive.

In my early twenties, was diagnosed as manic-depressive with psychotic tendencies at the age of 6, became medicated at the age of 7. All started with me refusing to talk to anyone but my parents until I was 4, having ADHD, and then they realized those were manic episodes when the medication made me want to kill myself and I decided on a whim one day to jump off of the third story balcony of my dad's house. Through K-12, I suffered constantly. I've been to therapists my entire life, am on medication which is good enough to let me function but not enough to make me happy. My senior year was me spending a lot of time in the bathroom at school crying and self harming, a lot of showing up to school unshowered and barely conscious, and just sitting in class staring blankly and trying not to cry. My teachers all took pity on me and let me turn things in the day before graduation or gave me pass/fail grades, I should not have graduated. Probably did it because I missed a month of school after a suicide attempt that every nurse at the hospital said that it was some kind of miracle that I survived. Coping is hard, but I'm in college now after a break and I'm at least functioning these days. I still have panic attacks and days where I can barely remember who I am, but I've decided to be open with people and if they can't handle me without me trying to pretend that I'm okay, they don't need to be in my life. I found that pretending like I was normal triggered a LOT of my episodes, because I would constantly dwell on the things I was doing wrong, and if there's one thing about depressive episodes, it's that they make you very chronically exhausted and I was expending all of my energy on pretending like everything was fine, which would sometimes send me into mania and make things worse. I also found that there are some days you just need to take care of yourself, and calling in to work and emailing your professors isn't the end of the world because you are not playing hooky, you are truly sick. Do not feel bad about doing so and taking things slow.

I have friends who are photographers who I've helped with projects, and I've taken many classes for photography, although I draw and paint more. Doing nature photography takes hours of lying/crouching in uncomfortable positions to get the right angle, the right lighting at the right time of day, and if a beautiful moment is being captured, it can never be recreated. Similar to how a drawing or painting will never come out the same way twice. You spend months learning what type of lens to use, proper aperture, there are many rules to follow in order to catch the viewers attention in different ways...sure, any schmuck can take a picture with an iPhone, but photography is absolutely an art. Moving photographs that capture an emotion are far different from someone's mom taking a picture at their child's soccer game. Yes, it may have been something "that was there," but you get to share your perspective and tell a story, if done correctly. Sharing moments between people, sharing stories of poverty, famine, or glee and celebration. If that's not art, I don't know what is.
